# Reactivity

Use the signals, computeds, operators and effects of nanoviews/store in views.

`nanoviews/store` is the reactive half of Nanoviews: it re-exports the signals that [Nano Kit](https://nano-kit.js.org/) is built on. A view is built once and never re-renders. It binds signals into its text, attributes and blocks, and each binding updates its own piece of the DOM when a signal it reads changes.

```ts
import { signal, computed } from 'nanoviews/store'
import { button, component$ } from 'nanoviews'

const Counter = component$(() => {
  const $count = signal(0)
  const $double = computed(() => $count() * 2)

  return (
    button({
      onClick() {
        $count(count => count + 1)
      }
    })(
      $count, ' doubled is ', $double
    )
  )
})

Counter()
// <button>0 doubled is 0</button>
// after a click: <button>1 doubled is 2</button>
```

`@nano_kit/store` is built on the same core, so the [Nano Kit store docs](https://nano-kit.js.org/store/core-concepts/) cover these primitives in more depth. This page shows them the way a view uses them.

## Signals

`signal` creates a writable signal with an initial value. Call it with no arguments to read the value, and with one argument to write it. A function passed as the new value is a reducer: it receives the current value and returns the next one.

```ts
import { signal } from 'nanoviews/store'

const $count = signal(0)

$count() // 0
$count(5)
$count(count => count + 1)
$count() // 6
```

A view takes the signal itself, not its value. A signal child is a text node that follows the signal, and a signal attribute keeps the attribute in sync:

```ts
import { signal } from 'nanoviews/store'
import { div, button, span, component$ } from 'nanoviews'

const Stepper = component$(() => {
  const $value = signal(1)

  return (
    div({
      'data-value': $value
    })(
      button({
        onClick() {
          $value(value => value - 1)
        }
      })(
        '-'
      ),
      span()($value),
      button({
        onClick() {
          $value(value => value + 1)
        }
      })(
        '+'
      )
    )
  )
})

Stepper()
// <div data-value="1"><button>-</button><span>1</span><button>+</button></div>
```

A click on `+` writes `2`, and both follow: `data-value="2"` and `<span>2</span>`. Called while the view is built, `span()($value())` would read the value once and show `1` forever. Blocks take signals the same way: `if_`, `show_` and `for_` follow the signal they are given.

`signal<T>()` without an initial value holds `undefined` and is typed `WritableSignal<T | undefined>`. The initial value is stored as it is, a function included, but a function written later is always a reducer, so a signal that holds a callback is written as `$onSave(() => save)`.

## Accessors

An accessor is any function that returns a value, `() => T`. A signal is an accessor, and so is an arrow that reads signals. A view treats every function child that is not a description or a component instance, and every function given to an attribute other than an `on*` handler, `ref` and `autoFocus`, as an accessor: a binding calls it, remembers the signals the call read, and calls it again when one of them changes.

```ts
import { signal } from 'nanoviews/store'
import { p, b, component$ } from 'nanoviews'

const Total = component$(() => {
  const $quantity = signal(3)
  const $price = signal(4.5)

  return (
    p({
      title: () => `${$quantity()} items`
    })(
      'Total: ', b()(() => ($quantity() * $price()).toFixed(2))
    )
  )
})

Total() // <p title="3 items">Total: <b>13.50</b></p>
```

An accessor is not cached: each binding runs it on its own, and again on every change of what it read. That suits an expression used once. A value read in several places, or costly to compute, belongs in a [computed](#computeds), and an expression that an [operator](#operators) covers takes the operator.

A component prop that may be static or reactive is typed `Signalish<T>`, which is `T | Accessor<T>`. Children, attributes, class lists and [operators](#operators) take both forms, so a component hands such a prop on as it came. Where it needs the value itself, `$get(value)` reads either form and tracks an accessor. The Components page shows both under Handing Props On, along with `style`, the one place where a prop does not go in as it came.

`get(value)` reads the same way as `$get`, without tracking. That matters only inside an effect, a computed or an accessor: a component body is not tracked, so a read there, `$user().id` say, happens once and nothing follows it.

## Computeds

`computed` derives a value from other signals and caches it. The body does not run until the computed is read, and runs again only when it is read after a dependency changed. While a binding or an effect follows it, it is kept up to date and notifies its readers only when its result changes.

```ts
import { signal, computed } from 'nanoviews/store'
import { p, component$ } from 'nanoviews'

interface Todo {
  title: string
  done: boolean
}

const $todos = signal<Todo[]>([
  { title: 'Write docs', done: false },
  { title: 'Ship it', done: false }
])
const $left = computed(() => $todos().filter(todo => !todo.done).length)

const Footer = component$(() => (
  p()(
    $left, ' left'
  )
))

Footer() // <p>2 left</p>
```

Renaming a todo writes a new array, so `$left` runs again, but its result is still `2` and the text node is left alone. Checking a todo off makes it `1`, and the text follows: `<p>1 left</p>`.

A computed is read-only: writing it is a type error. Keep its body pure, with no writes and no effects: it runs when something reads it, and the development build warns about an effect created inside it.

### `selector`

In a list that marks one row, the selected one say, a `computed` per row over the selected id would wake every row on each change, for two of them to change. `selector` turns this around: it reads the source once and wakes only the readers whose answer changed.

```ts
import { signal, selector } from 'nanoviews/store'
import { ul, li, for_, trackById } from 'nanoviews'

const $folders = signal([
  { id: 1, name: 'Inbox' },
  { id: 2, name: 'Drafts' },
  { id: 3, name: 'Sent' }
])
const $selectedId = signal(1)
const $isSelected = selector($selectedId)

ul()(
  for_($folders, trackById)(
    ($folder, $index, id) => li({
      class: () => $isSelected(id) && 'selected',
      onClick() {
        $selectedId(id)
      }
    })(
      () => $folder().name
    )
  )
)
// <ul><li class="selected">Inbox</li><li>Drafts</li><li>Sent</li></ul>
```

`selector($selectedId)` returns a function of a key. Called in a binding, an effect or a computed, `$isSelected(id)` subscribes the caller to that key alone: a click on `Sent` wakes the `Inbox` row, which loses the selection, and the `Sent` row, which gets it, and leaves `Drafts` alone. Called anywhere else, it just answers.

A second argument replaces the `key === value` test with any derivation: `selector($source, (key, value) => result)`. Such a selector asks every live key on each change, while the default test moves at most two, so keep the default where it fits.

## Operators

Most bindings are a short expression over a signal: a negation, a comparison, a fallback, a class that is there or not. The operators write such an expression without an arrow, and take static values and accessors alike. With an accessor among the operands an operator returns an accessor, which a view binds; with none it returns the plain result, which costs no binding at all.

```ts
import { type Signalish, signal, is } from 'nanoviews/store'

const $tab = signal('home')

is($tab, 'home') // Accessor<boolean>, follows $tab
is('home', 'home') // true

function isHome(tab: Signalish<string>) {
  return is(tab, 'home') // Signalish<boolean>
}
```

The result type, `Fop`, follows the same rule: an accessor when an operand is an accessor, the plain value when none can be, and `Signalish` when an operand may be either, like a `Signalish` prop. So a component hands its props to the operators as they came:

```ts
import { type Signalish, signal, gt, is, pick, text, when } from 'nanoviews/store'
import { span, component$ } from 'nanoviews'

const tones = {
  info: 'badge_info',
  alert: 'badge_alert'
}

interface BadgeProps {
  count: Signalish<number>
  tone?: Signalish<keyof typeof tones>
}

const Badge = component$(({ count, tone = 'info' }: BadgeProps) => (
  span({
    class: ['badge', pick(tones, tone), when(gt(count, 99), 'badge_wide')],
    hidden: is(count, 0),
    'aria-label': text`${count} unread`
  })(
    when(gt(count, 99), '99+', count)
  )
))

const $unread = signal(120)

Badge({
  count: 5
})
// <span class="badge badge_info" aria-label="5 unread">5</span>

Badge({
  count: $unread,
  tone: 'alert'
})
// <span class="badge badge_alert badge_wide" aria-label="120 unread">99+</span>
```

The first badge got static props only: every operator returned a plain value, and the span holds no binding. The second follows `$unread`.

| Operator                | Same as             |
| ----------------------- | ------------------- |
| `not(a)`                | `!a`                |
| `and(a, b)`             | `a && b`            |
| `or(a, b)`              | `a \|\| b`          |
| `every(a, b, ...)`      | `a && b && ...`     |
| `some(a, b, ...)`       | `a \|\| b \|\| ...` |
| `is(a, b)`              | `a === b`           |
| `isNot(a, b)`           | `a !== b`           |
| `gt(a, b)`, `gte(a, b)` | `a > b`, `a >= b`   |
| `lt(a, b)`, `lte(a, b)` | `a < b`, `a <= b`   |
| `when(a, b, c)`         | `a ? b : c`         |
| `pick(a, b)`            | `a[b]`              |
| ``text`a${b}` ``        | `` `a${b}` ``       |

- `and`, `or`, `every` and `some` return an operand, not a boolean, the way `&&` and `||` do: `and($active, 'active')` is `'active'` or the falsy value. A class that a condition switches on reads better as `when($active, 'active')`.
- `gt`, `gte`, `lt` and `lte` compare numbers.
- `when` without its third operand gives `undefined` for a falsy condition, which removes an attribute and drops a class list part. Passed straight as a child, it takes the third operand, `when($done, 'Done', null)`: without one, TypeScript rejects the call.
- `pick` reads a key of an object or an index of an array; an empty key, `null` or `undefined`, picks `undefined`, which suits an optional prop. A `null` collection throws: read a nullable object through a [record](#other-exports), whose children read `undefined`, or an arrow with `?.`.
- `text` builds a string from strings, numbers, booleans and bigints; `null` and `undefined` add nothing. A template string in a view reads its signals once, while the view is built, and `text` keeps the string bound.

An operator's accessor is not cached: it runs on every read, like an arrow. Wrap it in `computed` when the value is shared or costly: `computed(and(gt($age, 17), $hasLicense))`.

## Effects

Nanoviews has two effects with the same body. `effect` from `nanoviews/store` is the store effect: it runs at once, wherever it is called, and returns a function that stops it. `effect$` from `nanoviews` is the component effect: it belongs to the view being built, first runs once its tree is in the document, and stops when its part of the view is removed. Components covers `effect$` in full.

```ts
import { signal, effect } from 'nanoviews/store'
import { div, component$, effect$ } from 'nanoviews'

const $theme = signal('light')

// A store effect: runs now and on every change of $theme, until stop()
const stop = effect(() => {
  document.documentElement.dataset.theme = $theme()
})

const Panel = component$(() => {
  const $panel = signal<HTMLDivElement | null>(null)

  // A component effect: first runs once the panel is in the document
  effect$(() => {
    console.log('Panel width:', $panel()?.offsetWidth)
  })

  return (
    div({
      ref: $panel
    })(
      'Panel'
    )
  )
})
```

|                        | `effect`                                                                        | `effect$`                           |
| ---------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------- |
| Imported from          | `nanoviews/store`                                                               | `nanoviews`                         |
| Called                 | anywhere                                                                        | while a view is built under `mount` |
| First run              | at once                                                                         | once the tree is in the document    |
| Under a hidden `show_` | keeps running                                                                   | cleaned up, runs again on show      |
| Stopped by             | the returned function, or the removal of the part of the view it was created in | the removal of its part of the view |

Use `effect$` in components and `effect` in stores: module-level code and the factories of dependency injection run outside the scope of any view, and `effect$` throws there. For the same reason, an `effect` in a factory is tied to no view, even when a render injected the factory, and no unmount stops it (see Factories Use `effect`). An `effect` in a component works too, with the differences the table shows: it runs before anything is in the document, and a hidden `show_` does not pause it.

## Other Exports

The exports below work the same in a view as anywhere else. Nano Kit's store docs cover them in depth:

| Export                                                                      | What it does                                                                                                           | Nano Kit docs                                                                                                                |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `batch(fn)`                                                                 | holds the flush until `fn` returns, so several writes update the view once                                             | [Batching Updates](https://nano-kit.js.org/store/core-concepts/#batching-updates)                                            |
| `trigger(fn)`, `trigger($x)`                                                | notifies the readers with no new value, after an array or an object was changed in place                               | [Manual Trigger](https://nano-kit.js.org/store/core-concepts/#manual-trigger)                                                |
| `untracked(fn)`                                                             | runs `fn` without subscribing the caller to what it reads                                                              | [Using `untracked`](https://nano-kit.js.org/store/core-concepts/#using-untracked)                                            |
| `action(fn)`                                                                | wraps a function so that everything it reads is untracked                                                              | [Actions](https://nano-kit.js.org/store/core-concepts/#actions)                                                              |
| `effectScope(fn)`                                                           | groups the effects created in `fn` and returns one function that stops them all                                        | [Effect Scope](https://nano-kit.js.org/store/advanced/#effect-scope)                                                         |
| `composeDestroys(...fns)`                                                   | merges several cleanups into one                                                                                       | [Cleanup Composition](https://nano-kit.js.org/store/advanced/#cleanup-composition)                                           |
| `subscribe`, `listen`, `observe`, `subscribeAny`                            | low-level effects that hand the value to a callback                                                                    | [Subscribe, Listen, and Observe](https://nano-kit.js.org/store/advanced/#subscribe-listen-and-observe)                       |
| `length($x)`, `boolean($x)`                                                 | cached computeds of the length and of the truthiness; they take an accessor only, `pick(items, 'length')` takes either | [Computed Properties](https://nano-kit.js.org/store/advanced/#computed-properties)                                           |
| `push`, `pop`, `shift`, `unshift`, `setIndex`, `deleteIndex`, `updateArray` | write a changed copy of an array and return what the array method returns                                              | [Array Operations](https://nano-kit.js.org/store/advanced/#array-operations)                                                 |
| `record($x)`, `deepRecord($x)`                                              | a child signal for every property of an object signal, at the top level or at every depth                              | [Record](https://nano-kit.js.org/store/advanced/#record), [Deep Record](https://nano-kit.js.org/store/advanced/#deep-record) |
| `atIndex($list, index)`                                                     | a writable child signal at an index, which may be a signal                                                             | [Array Operations](https://nano-kit.js.org/store/advanced/#array-operations)                                                 |
| `setKey`, `deleteKey`                                                       | write a changed copy of an object                                                                                      | [Object Operations](https://nano-kit.js.org/store/advanced/#object-operations)                                               |
| `atKey($map, key)`                                                          | a writable child signal at a key, which may be a signal                                                                | [Object Operations](https://nano-kit.js.org/store/advanced/#object-operations)                                               |
| `child`                                                                     | the low-level form of `atIndex` and `atKey`                                                                            | [Child Signals](https://nano-kit.js.org/store/low-level/#child-signals)                                                      |
| `resolved(source)`                                                          | the result, the error and the pending flag of a promise                                                                | [Async State](https://nano-kit.js.org/store/advanced/#async-state)                                                           |
| `task($x, work)`, `waitTasks($x)`                                           | attach async work to a signal, and wait until it settles                                                               | [Waiting for Async Operations](https://nano-kit.js.org/store/testing/#waiting-for-async-operations)                          |
| `mountable($x)`, `onMount($x, fn)`                                          | a lazy store: `fn` runs when the first reader arrives, and what it returns runs after the last one is gone             | [Mountable Stores](https://nano-kit.js.org/store/core-concepts/#mountable-stores)                                            |
| `STORE_UNMOUNT_DELAY`                                                       | the delay before a lazy store unmounts                                                                                 | [Debounced Unmounting](https://nano-kit.js.org/store/core-concepts/#debounced-unmounting)                                    |
| `onMountEffect`, `onMountEffectScope`                                       | an effect or an effect scope that runs only while a signal is mounted                                                  | [onMountEffect and onMountEffectScope](https://nano-kit.js.org/store/advanced/#onmounteffect-and-onmounteffectscope)         |
| `onStart`, `onStop`, `onMounted`                                            | the mount events of a mountable signal, without the delay of `onMount`                                                 | [Lifecycle Hooks](https://nano-kit.js.org/store/low-level/#lifecycle-hooks)                                                  |
| `start($x)`, `exec($x)`                                                     | mount a signal by hand and keep it mounted, or mount it for one read                                                   | [Triggering Mount Events](https://nano-kit.js.org/store/testing/#triggering-mount-events)                                    |
| `isMounted($x)`                                                             | whether a mountable signal is mounted now                                                                              | —                                                                                                                            |
| `isAccessor`, `isSignal`, `isEmpty`, `isFunction`                           | type checks of a value                                                                                                 | [Type Checking](https://nano-kit.js.org/store/advanced/#type-checking)                                                       |
| `isWritable`, `isMountable`                                                 | type checks of a signal                                                                                                | [Type Checking](https://nano-kit.js.org/store/low-level/#type-checking)                                                      |
| `toSignal`, `toAccessor`, `toAccessorOrSignal`                              | conversions of a value or an accessor to a signal or an accessor                                                       | [Value Extraction](https://nano-kit.js.org/store/advanced/#value-extraction)                                                 |
| `noop`, `identity`                                                          | shared helper functions                                                                                                | [Reusable Helpers](https://nano-kit.js.org/store/advanced/#reusable-helpers)                                                 |

## Dependency Injection

`inject`, `provide`, `provideAs`, `InjectionContext`, `Injectable$` and `DependencyNotFound` come from `nanoviews/store` as well: dependency injection is how views share stores. A view opens a context with `context$`, and its components inject stores from it during render. Dependency Injection covers it.

## Types

Import these types from `nanoviews/store`: `nanoviews` itself does not export `Accessor`, `ReadableSignal`, `WritableSignal` or `Signalish`.

| Type                | What it is                                                            |
| ------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Accessor<T>`       | `() => T`: a signal, a computed or a plain function                   |
| `ReadableSignal<T>` | a signal that can be read: a computed, a child of a computed          |
| `WritableSignal<T>` | a signal that can be written as well                                  |
| `Signalish<T>`      | `T \| Accessor<T>`: a static value or an accessor, the type of a prop |
| `SignalishValue<S>` | the value type of a `Signalish`                                       |
| `EmptyValue`        | `undefined \| null \| void`                                           |
| `FalsyValue`        | `EmptyValue \| false \| '' \| 0`                                      |
| `Destroy`           | `() => void`: a stop or a cleanup function                            |
| `EffectCallback`    | the body of an effect: `(warmup?: true) => Destroy \| void`           |
| `Mountable<S>`      | a signal marked with `mountable`                                      |
| `Resolved<T>`       | the tuple `resolved` returns                                          |
| `Injectable<T>`     | a factory or a class for `inject`                                     |
| `Fop<Operands, R>`  | what an operator returns for its operands                             |

A prop typed `Accessor<T>` or `WritableSignal<T>` is always reactive, so its name takes the `$`, like `$items: Accessor<Item[]>`; a `Signalish<T>` prop keeps a plain name.

## Beyond `nanoviews/store`

`nanoviews/store` is the reactive core alone. [`@nano_kit/store`](https://nano-kit.js.org/store/) re-exports the same core and adds rate limiting (`pace`, `paced`, `debounce`, `throttle`), `previous`, `latest`, `interval`, `SignalsMap`, codecs, storage-backed signals and SSR hydration. Its signals are those of `nanoviews/store`, so a view binds them like its own: install `@nano_kit/store` next to `nanoviews` and import the extras from it.

> Caution: Nanoviews and the `@nano_kit/*` packages have to share one copy of this core. Nanoviews and Nano Kit says what breaks with two copies and how to merge them.

---

# Components

Build reusable views with component$: props, children, render props, effects with effect$, slots and polymorphic components.

Components are the building blocks of an application: reusable pieces of view that take props and children the way an element takes attributes and children. A component renders once, when its instance is built. Its state lives in signals, and the DOM follows them through bindings instead of re-rendering.

## `component$`

`component$` creates a component from a render function. The component takes its props in the first call and its children in the second, like an element does, and the children call is optional. The render gets the props and the children and returns what to show, anything a child can be: a description, a node, a primitive or a signal.

```ts
import { type Attributes, div, b, component$ } from 'nanoviews'

const Card = component$((props: Attributes<'div'>, children) => (
  div(props)(
    'Card: ',
    ...children.length ? children : ['empty']
  )
))

Card()
// <div>Card: empty</div>

Card({
  class: 'card'
})(
  'Hello, ', b()('Nanoviews')
)
// <div class="card">Card: Hello, <b>Nanoviews</b></div>
```

The props argument is optional when every prop is, as here. Type the props on the parameter of the render rather than as a type argument of `component$`: the component's types are read off the render, as [Components Without Children](#components-without-children) shows.

## Props

A prop is a plain value or a signal, and a component is written so that it does not need to know which.

### Plain Values and Signals

Type a prop `Signalish<T>` when either form is fine, `Accessor<T>` for read-only reactive input, and `WritableSignal<T>` for state the component writes back. A prop typed as an accessor or a signal is always reactive, so its name takes the `$`, like a signal's; a `Signalish` prop keeps a plain name. The types come from `nanoviews/store`.

```ts
import { type Accessor, type Signalish, type WritableSignal, signal, computed, length } from 'nanoviews/store'
import { label, input, component$ } from 'nanoviews'

interface SearchProps {
  placeholder?: Signalish<string>
  $query: WritableSignal<string>
  $count: Accessor<number>
}

const Search = component$(({ placeholder, $query, $count }: SearchProps) => (
  label()(
    input({
      type: 'search',
      placeholder,
      value: $query
    }),
    ' Found: ', $count
  )
))

const players = ['chopper', 'magixx', 'donk']
const $query = signal('')
const $found = computed(() => players.filter(name => name.includes($query())))

Search({
  placeholder: 'Player',
  $query,
  $count: length($found)
})
// <label><input type="search" placeholder="Player"> Found: 3</label>
```

`value: $query` binds the input both ways, so typing `do` writes the query, and the count follows: `Found: 1`.

The render runs once, and a call in it reads the value once: `$query()` in the render body would freeze the query it held at build time. Pass a signal on as it is, or read it inside an accessor, a handler or an effect.

### Handing Props On

Destructure the props and hand them on as they came. An attribute, a child and a part of a class list take a plain value and a signal alike, and so do the operators of `nanoviews/store` such as `text`, `when`, `is` and `pick`, which return a plain value when none of their operands is a signal or an accessor:

```ts
import { type Signalish, text } from 'nanoviews/store'
import { type Attributes, button, component$ } from 'nanoviews'

interface ButtonProps extends Attributes<'button'> {
  size?: Signalish<'s' | 'm'>
}

const Button = component$((
  {
    size = 'm',
    class: className,
    ...props
  }: ButtonProps,
  children
) => (
  button({
    class: ['button', text`button_${size}`, className],
    ...props
  })(
    ...children
  )
))

Button({
  size: 's',
  id: 'send',
  class: 'wide'
})(
  'Send'
)
// <button class="button button_s wide" id="send">Send</button>
```

Given a signal, the same render binds the class to it:

```ts
import { signal } from 'nanoviews/store'

const $size = signal<'s' | 'm'>('m')

Button({
  size: $size
})(
  'Send'
)
// <button class="button button_m">Send</button>

$size('s')
// <button class="button button_s">Send</button>
```

Where the current value is needed rather than bound, in a handler or an effect, `$get(prop)` reads it in either form. An expression the operators do not cover reads the prop the same way inside an accessor:

```ts
import { type Signalish, signal, $get } from 'nanoviews/store'
import { button, span, component$ } from 'nanoviews'

const Counter = component$(({ step = 1 }: { step?: Signalish<number> }) => {
  const $count = signal(0)

  return (
    button({
      onClick() {
        $count(count => count + $get(step))
      }
    })(
      'Count: ', $count
    )
  )
})

const Price = component$(({ amount }: { amount: Signalish<number> }) => (
  span()(
    '$', () => $get(amount).toFixed(2)
  )
))

Price({
  amount: 5
})
// <span>$5.00</span>
```

`style` is the one place a prop does not go in as it is. The values of a style object are plain, so a `Signalish` prop goes in through an accessor of the whole object: `style: () => ({ '--columns': $get(columns) })`, as in the next example.

### Element Attributes

A component that passes arbitrary attributes on to its element types its props as `Attributes<'tag'>` extended with its own, and spreads the rest onto the element. Two things go with the spread:

- The `class` it received is folded into its own class list: left in the rest, it would replace the component's own. A list may hold another list or an accessor, so `class: ['grid', className]` takes whatever the caller gave.
- Every prop that is not an attribute is taken out first. TypeScript does not check a spread for unknown keys, and a prop left in the rest is written to the element as an attribute.

```ts
import { type Signalish, $get } from 'nanoviews/store'
import { type Attributes, div, component$ } from 'nanoviews'

interface GridProps extends Attributes<'div'> {
  columns?: Signalish<number>
}

const Grid = component$((
  {
    columns = 3,
    class: className,
    ...props
  }: GridProps,
  children
) => (
  div({
    class: ['grid', className],
    style: () => ({
      '--columns': $get(columns)
    }),
    ...props
  })(
    ...children
  )
))

Grid({
  columns: 2,
  class: 'gallery'
})(
  'Photos'
)
// <div class="grid gallery" style="--columns: 2;">Photos</div>
```

`columns` stays out of `props` because it is destructured; left in, it would land on the element as `columns="2"`.

## Children

`children` is always an array, empty when the instance was not called with children, so the render can spread it or check its length. Untyped, the children are `Child[]`, anything an element takes. They are typed on the second parameter of the render, the way the props are typed on the first.

### Render Props

A tuple with a function makes a render prop: the caller passes a function, and the component calls it with data of its own.

```ts
import { type Child, for_, ul, li, b, component$ } from 'nanoviews'

const List = component$((
  { items }: { items: string[] },
  [renderItem]: [renderItem: (item: string) => Child]
) => (
  ul()(
    for_(items)(
      item => li()(renderItem(item))
    )
  )
))

List({
  items: ['chopper', 'magixx']
})(
  item => b()(
    'Player: ', item
  )
)
// <ul><li><b>Player: chopper</b></li><li><b>Player: magixx</b></li></ul>
```

`for_` renders the plain array of the prop once, with no tracker (see Static Arrays).

### Instances Only

`children: ComponentInstance[]` suits a component that wraps every child in markup of its own: it takes instances, and a string, a signal or a DOM node is a type error. An element description such as `div()` and a slot instance have the shape of an instance and pass too.

```ts
import { type Attributes, type ComponentInstance, for_, menu, li, button, component$ } from 'nanoviews'

const ToolButton = component$((props: Attributes<'button'>, children) => button(props)(...children))

const Toolbar = component$((
  props: Attributes<'menu'>,
  children: ComponentInstance[]
) => (
  menu(props)(
    for_(children)(
      child => li()(child)
    )
  )
))

Toolbar()(
  ToolButton()('Bold'),
  ToolButton()('Italic')
)
// <menu><li><button>Bold</button></li><li><button>Italic</button></li></menu>

Toolbar()('Bold') // type error: Argument of type 'string' is not assignable to parameter of type 'ComponentInstance'.
```

### Components Without Children

A render with no `children` parameter makes a component that takes none, so children passed to it are a type error rather than lost. The same goes for a slot made with [`slot$`](#slots).

```ts
import { type Attributes, hr, component$ } from 'nanoviews'

const Divider = component$((props: Attributes<'hr'>) => hr(props))

Divider({
  class: 'wide'
})
// <hr class="wide">

Divider()('Hello') // type error: Expected 0 arguments, but got 1.
```

That is read off the render itself, so it needs the types inferred. With the type arguments written out, `component$<Props>(...)` keeps the children allowed, and `component$<Props, []>(...)` turns them off:

```ts
const Loose = component$<Attributes<'hr'>>(props => hr(props))
const Strict = component$<Attributes<'hr'>, []>(props => hr(props))

Loose()('Hello') // compiles, and the children are dropped
Strict()('Hello') // type error: Expected 0 arguments, but got 1.
```

## `effect$`

`effect$` adds an effect to the view being built. It first runs once its part of the view is in the document, which at mount means once `mount` has appended the whole tree, so measuring and focusing are safe on the first run. It re-runs when a signal it read changes, and it is stopped when its part of the view is removed. A function it returns is the cleanup: it runs before each re-run and when the effect is stopped.

```ts
import { signal } from 'nanoviews/store'
import { span, component$, effect$ } from 'nanoviews'

const $interval = signal(1000)

const Ticker = component$(() => {
  const $ticks = signal(0)

  effect$(() => {
    const id = setInterval(() => {
      $ticks(ticks => ticks + 1)
    }, $interval())

    return () => clearInterval(id)
  })

  return (
    span()(
      'Ticks: ', $ticks
    )
  )
})
```

The effect reads `$interval`, so a new interval restarts the timer, and the cleanup clears the old one first. Unmounting the ticker clears the last one.

An effect that reads no signal runs once after mount and cleans up on unmount, which makes it a mount and unmount hook:

```ts
import { div, component$, effect$ } from 'nanoviews'

const Hello = component$(() => {
  effect$(() => {
    console.log('Mounted')

    return () => console.log('Unmounted')
  })

  return div()('Hello, Nanoviews!')
})
```

`effect$` belongs to the scope of the view being built, so it is called while a view is built under `mount`: in a render, in a branch of a block, in a row of a list. At module level, in an event handler or in a dependency factory there is no such scope, and it throws.

### `warmup`

The effect function receives `warmup`: `true` on the first run and `undefined` on a re-run caused by a change, so the body can tell the two apart.

```ts
import { signal } from 'nanoviews/store'
import { input, component$, effect$ } from 'nanoviews'

const SearchField = component$(() => {
  const $query = signal('')

  effect$((warmup) => {
    const query = $query()

    if (!warmup) {
      console.log('Query changed:', query)
    }
  })

  return (
    input({
      type: 'search',
      value: $query
    })
  )
})
```

Content hidden by `show_` has its effects cleaned up, and showing it again runs them with `warmup` set once more.

### Store Effects

`effect` from `nanoviews/store` is the store effect. It runs at once wherever it is called and returns a function that stops it. Called in a render, it is still stopped on unmount, but it runs before the tree is built, and a hidden `show_` does not pause it. Views use `effect$`; stores and dependency factories use `effect`, as Reactivity shows.

## Slots

A layout with several places to fill, such as a header and a footer around the content, takes them as slots. A slot is a component made with `slot$`: its instances name the slot they belong to and keep their props, so a layout can pick them out of its children. `slots$` declares the slots a layout takes and gives its render the declared slots in order, an instance or `undefined` each, followed by the rest of the children. `component$` turns the result into a component.

```ts
import { type Attributes, main, header, footer, component$, slot$, slots$ } from 'nanoviews'

const LayoutHeader = slot$((props: Attributes<'header'>, children) => header(props)(...children))
const LayoutFooter = slot$((props: Attributes<'footer'>, children) => footer(props)(...children))

const Layout = component$(slots$(
  [LayoutHeader, LayoutFooter],
  (props: Attributes<'main'>, headerSlot, footerSlot, children) => (
    main(props)(
      headerSlot,
      ...children,
      footerSlot
    )
  )
))

Layout({
  class: 'page'
})(
  LayoutHeader({
    class: 'header'
  })(
    'Header content'
  ),
  'Main content',
  LayoutFooter({
    class: 'footer'
  })(
    'Footer content'
  )
)
// <main class="page"><header class="header">Header content</header>Main content<footer class="footer">Footer content</footer></main>
```

The caller passes the slots in any order, among the other children; the layout places them where it wants.

### Missing, Repeated and Undeclared Slots

A slot the caller did not pass is `undefined` and renders nothing. The same slot passed twice keeps the last one:

```ts
Layout()(
  'Main content',
  LayoutFooter()('First'),
  LayoutFooter()('Second')
)
// <main>Main content<footer>Second</footer></main>
```

A slot the layout did not declare would have nowhere to go, so it throws when the layout renders. Declare every slot a caller may pass:

```ts
const HeaderOnly = component$(slots$(
  [LayoutHeader],
  (props: Attributes<'main'>, headerSlot, children) => (
    main(props)(
      headerSlot,
      ...children
    )
  )
))

HeaderOnly()(
  LayoutFooter()('Footer content')
)
// throws on build: Error: Slot is not declared in slots$
```

### Slot Instances

A slot instance without the children call is a slot with no children, and a slot instance outside a `slots$` layout is an ordinary component instance that renders where it stands:

```ts
import { div } from 'nanoviews'

Layout()(
  LayoutHeader({
    class: 'header'
  }),
  'Main content'
)
// <main><header class="header"></header>Main content</main>

div()(
  LayoutHeader()('On its own')
)
// <div><header>On its own</header></div>
```

### Handing Data to a Slot

A slot renders inside the layout's tree, after the layout's render, so the layout hands it data the way a parent hands data to any child: with `context$`, which the slot reads with `inject`. When the caller's markup in the slot needs that data, the slot takes a render function as its child:

```ts
import { type WritableSignal, signal, provide, inject, not } from 'nanoviews/store'
import { type Attributes, type Child, div, footer, textarea, button, component$, context$, slot$, slots$ } from 'nanoviews'

function Draft$() {
  return signal('')
}

const EditorFooter = slot$((
  props: Attributes<'footer'>,
  [render]: [render: ($draft: WritableSignal<string>) => Child]
) => {
  const $draft = inject(Draft$)

  return (
    footer(props)(
      render($draft)
    )
  )
})

const Editor = component$(slots$(
  [EditorFooter],
  (props: Attributes<'div'>, footerSlot, children) => {
    const $draft = signal('')

    return (
      context$(provide(Draft$, $draft))(
        div(props)(
          ...children,
          textarea({
            value: $draft
          }),
          footerSlot
        )
      )
    )
  }
))

Editor()(
  'Comment',
  EditorFooter()(
    $draft => button({
      disabled: not($draft)
    })(
      'Send'
    )
  )
)
// <div>Comment<textarea></textarea><footer><button disabled="true">Send</button></footer></div>
```

The button is disabled while the draft is empty and enabled once something is typed.

## Polymorphic Components

A component that renders the element or the component its caller picks is made with `polymorphic$`. Its props extend `PolymorphicProps` of the default target, given by its tag name, which brings the `as` prop and the attributes of that element. The render sets the default of `as` and passes the rest on:

```ts
import { type PolymorphicProps, a, button, polymorphic$ } from 'nanoviews'

interface ButtonProps extends PolymorphicProps<'button'> {
  variant?: 'primary' | 'secondary'
}

const Button = polymorphic$((
  {
    as = button,
    variant = 'primary',
    class: className,
    ...props
  }: ButtonProps,
  children
) => (
  as({
    class: ['button', `button_${variant}`, className],
    ...props
  })(
    ...children
  )
))

Button({
  type: 'submit'
})(
  'Save'
)
// <button class="button button_primary" type="submit">Save</button>

Button({
  as: a,
  href: '/docs/'
})(
  'Read the docs'
)
// <a class="button button_primary" href="/docs/">Read the docs</a>

Button({
  href: '/docs/' // type error: a button takes no `href`
})
```

The props follow the target in `as`: with `as: a` they are those of a link, and without `as` those of a `button`, so `href` is a type error. `as` takes a component too, and brings its props:

```ts
import { type Attributes, a, component$ } from 'nanoviews'

const Link = component$((
  {
    to,
    ...props
  }: { to: string } & Attributes<'a'>,
  children
) => (
  a({
    href: to,
    ...props
  })(
    ...children
  )
))

Button({
  as: Link,
  to: '/home'
})(
  'Home'
)
// <a href="/home" class="button button_primary">Home</a>
```

The default target can be a component as well: `PolymorphicProps<typeof Link>` in the props, `as = Link` in the render. A void element, such as `input`, is no target, since it takes no children. A prop of the component's own may take the name of an attribute, the way a kit has a `color` of its own: declared again with a type of its own, it stays the component's prop whatever the target.

A second type argument of `PolymorphicProps` limits `as` to the targets it names, the default one aside:

```ts
import { type PolymorphicProps, article, div, span, polymorphic$ } from 'nanoviews'

const Paper = polymorphic$((
  {
    as = div,
    ...props
  }: PolymorphicProps<'div', 'section' | 'article' | 'aside'>,
  children
) => (
  as(props)(
    ...children
  )
))

Paper({
  as: article
})(
  'Letter'
)
// <article>Letter</article>

Paper({
  as: span // type error: a span is not among the targets
})
```

---

# Control Flow

Render conditions, cases and lists that follow signals.

A view is built once. A ternary or a `.map()` in it runs once, at build time, and nothing follows the signal it read. A condition or a list that changes needs a block: a call that takes a signal and keeps its part of the DOM in step with it. Blocks end with `_`.

| Block                           | Use when                              | Shape                                                                                   |
| ------------------------------- | ------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| [`if_`](#if_)                   | branch, rebuilt on every flip         | `if_($cond)(v => thenView, () => elseView)`                                             |
| [`show_`](#show_)               | toggle visibility, keep state and DOM | `show_($cond, () => view)`                                                              |
| [`switch_`](#switch_)           | one primitive value, several cases    | `switch_($tab)(case_('a', () => ...), default_(() => ...))`                             |
| [`match_`](#match_)             | first truthy condition wins           | `match_(when_($loading, () => ...), when_($error, $error => ...), default_(() => ...))` |
| [`show_switch_`](#show_switch_) | `switch_` that keeps every case alive | `show_switch_($tab)(case_('a', () => ...), default_(() => ...))`                        |
| [`show_match_`](#show_match_)   | `match_` that keeps every case alive  | `show_match_(when_($loading, () => ...), default_(() => ...))`                          |
| [`swap_`](#swap_)               | custom mapping value to view          | `swap_($value, value => view)`                                                          |
| [`for_`](#for_)                 | reactive list                         | `for_($items, trackById)(($item, $index, key) => row, () => emptyView)`                 |

Every block takes a plain value as well as a signal or an accessor. A plain value never changes, so the block decides once, at build time, and follows nothing. The children of a block are functions: the block calls one when it needs that child built.

## `if_`

`if_` renders one of two branches by the truthiness of a value: the first while it is truthy, the second while it is falsy.

```ts
import { signal } from 'nanoviews/store'
import { if_, b, i } from 'nanoviews'

const $open = signal(false)

if_($open)(
  () => b()('Open'),
  () => i()('Closed')
)
// <i>Closed</i>

$open(true)
// <b>Open</b>
```

The second branch is optional: without it a falsy value renders nothing.

### Narrowed Value

Each branch receives the value `if_` was given, typed to its side: the first branch gets the signal typed as truthy, so a nullable value needs no check inside it. The branch reads the signal live.

```ts
import { signal } from 'nanoviews/store'
import { if_, p } from 'nanoviews'

interface User {
  name: string
}

const $user = signal<User | null>(null)

if_($user)(
  $user => p()(
    'Hello, ', () => $user().name
  ),
  () => p()('Nobody is signed in')
)
// <p>Nobody is signed in</p>

$user({ name: 'Ann' })
// <p>Hello, Ann</p>

$user({ name: 'Bob' })
// <p>Hello, Bob</p>
```

### Rebuilt on a Flip

`if_` follows the truthiness of the value, not the value. A write that keeps it truthy, like the switch from Ann to Bob above, reaches the branch through its bindings: the same `p` stays and only its text changes. A flip rebuilds: the old branch is destroyed, and the new one starts from scratch, with new DOM and new local signals. A subtree that must keep its state across flips belongs in [`show_`](#show_).

### Plain Value

A plain value picks the branch once, at build time: `if_(isAdmin)(() => li()('Settings'))` renders the item or nothing and subscribes to nothing. The branch gets the plain value, narrowed the same way.

## `show_`

`show_` hides and shows a child instead of rebuilding it. The child is built once, when the block is built, even if the value is falsy then. Hiding parks the tree instead of destroying it:

- The nodes leave the document and are kept: showing puts the same nodes back.
- Local state is kept: the signals the render created live on.
- Bindings keep updating: text, attributes and `style` follow their signals while hidden, so the tree comes back up to date.
- `effect$` effects stop: their cleanups run on hide, while the DOM is still attached, and they run again on show, with `warmup` set to `true` as on the first run.

There is no else branch.

```ts
import { signal } from 'nanoviews/store'
import { show_, button } from 'nanoviews'

const $visible = signal(true)

show_($visible, () => {
  const $count = signal(0)

  return (
    button({
      onClick() {
        $count(count => count + 1)
      }
    })(
      'Count: ', $count
    )
  )
})
// <button>Count: 0</button>
```

The counter above keeps counting from where it was left: with `if_` it would start from zero every time it comes back.

Only the `effect$` effects stop. A timer started in one is cleared on hide and started again on show, and the count it drives is kept:

```ts
import { signal } from 'nanoviews/store'
import { show_, span, effect$, component$ } from 'nanoviews'

const Stopwatch = component$(() => {
  const $seconds = signal(0)

  effect$(() => {
    const id = setInterval(() => $seconds(seconds => seconds + 1), 1000)

    return () => clearInterval(id)
  })

  return (
    span()(
      $seconds, 's'
    )
  )
})

const $visible = signal(true)

show_($visible, () => Stopwatch())
// <span>0s</span>
```

A plain value renders the child or nothing: `show_(false, render)` never calls `render`.

> Keep portals and refs out of show\_: Hiding runs the cleanups a `portal` and a `ref` register, the way it runs those of `effect$`: the portal removes its content, the `ref` receives `null`, and showing again restores neither. Put the `show_` inside the portal instead, `portal(() => document.body, show_($open, () => Modal()))`: the parked DOM leaves the target and comes back with its state. A subtree that needs a live `ref` belongs in `if_`. See `portal`.

## `switch_`

`switch_` renders the case that equals a value. Cases are made with `case_(value, render)` and compared by strict equality; `default_(render)` answers when no case matches, and without it nothing renders.

```ts
import { signal } from 'nanoviews/store'
import { switch_, case_, default_, b } from 'nanoviews'

const $state = signal<'loading' | 'error' | 'done'>('loading')

switch_($state)(
  case_('loading', () => b()('Loading')),
  case_('error', () => b()('Error')),
  default_(() => 'Success')
)
// <b>Loading</b>

$state('done')
// Success
```

Case values are plain values, fixed when the block is built, and typed by the value: with the signal above, `case_('ready', ...)` is a type error. The child is built anew on every change of the value, the way [`swap_`](#swap_) builds it: a write from one unmatched value to another builds the `default_` child again. [`show_switch_`](#show_switch_) keeps every case alive instead.

## `match_`

`match_` renders the child of the first case that holds: a cascade of conditions written as a list instead of `if_` inside `if_` inside `if_`. Cases are made with `when_(value, render)`, and `default_`, the same one `switch_` takes, answers when no case holds.

```ts
import { signal } from 'nanoviews/store'
import { match_, when_, default_, b, i } from 'nanoviews'

const $loading = signal(true)
const $error = signal(false)

match_(
  when_($loading, () => i()('Loading')),
  when_($error, () => b()('Error')),
  default_(() => 'Ready')
)
// <i>Loading</i>

$loading(false)
// Ready
```

The walk stops at the case that holds, so a case below it is never read, and never wakes the block when it changes: while `$loading` is `true`, a write to `$error` does nothing. The child is rebuilt only when another case starts to hold. The list is fixed when the block is built, and the first `default_` in it is the one that answers.

### Conditions That Move Together

Cases that move together are worth a `batch`: without one every write swaps the content, so the case in between is built and started only to be replaced. Here, from `Loading`, the first write alone would render `Ready` and the second `Error`:

```ts
import { batch } from 'nanoviews/store'

batch(() => {
  $loading(false)
  $error(true)
})
// <b>Error</b>
```

### The Case Value

Every case hands its own value to its child: the signal it tested, which the child reads live.

```ts
import { signal } from 'nanoviews/store'
import { match_, when_, default_, b } from 'nanoviews'

interface Post {
  title: string
}

const $post = signal<Post | null>(null)

match_(
  when_($post, $post => b()(() => $post().title)),
  default_(() => 'No post')
)
// No post

$post({ title: 'Hello' })
// <b>Hello</b>
```

## `show_switch_`

`show_switch_` is `switch_` built on `show_`: every case is built once, up front, and the cases that do not match are parked, so a case comes back exactly as it was left. It takes the same `case_` and `default_`.

```ts
import { signal } from 'nanoviews/store'
import { show_switch_, case_, default_, button, b } from 'nanoviews'

const $tab = signal('counter')

show_switch_($tab)(
  case_('counter', () => {
    const $count = signal(0)

    return (
      button({
        onClick() {
          $count(count => count + 1)
        }
      })(
        'Count: ', $count
      )
    )
  }),
  default_(() => b()('Settings'))
)
// <button>Count: 0</button>

$tab('settings')
// <b>Settings</b>
```

The counter keeps its count while another tab is open: with `switch_` it would start from zero every time its tab comes back. A parked case follows the rules of `show_`: its bindings keep it up to date, its `effect$` effects run only while it is shown, and a `portal` or a live `ref` does not belong in it. A write that keeps the same case matching wakes no case, and a plain value builds the matching case alone.

## `show_match_`

`show_match_` is `match_` built on `show_`: the first case that holds is shown and every other case is parked. It takes the same `when_` and `default_` and walks the cases the same way, so cases that move together are worth a `batch` here too.

```ts
import { signal } from 'nanoviews/store'
import { show_match_, when_, default_, b, i } from 'nanoviews'

const $loading = signal(true)
const $error = signal(false)

show_match_(
  when_($loading, () => i()('Loading')),
  when_($error, () => b()('Error')),
  default_(() => 'Ready')
)
// <i>Loading</i>
```

A case child takes no value. It is built before its case holds and lives on, parked, after the case stops holding, so a value narrowed to the truthy side would not hold for it, and TypeScript turns such a child away. Read the signal itself instead, and let the read allow for the falsy side:

```ts
import { signal } from 'nanoviews/store'
import { show_match_, when_, default_, b } from 'nanoviews'

interface Post {
  title: string
}

const $post = signal<Post | null>(null)

show_match_(
  when_($post, $post => b()(() => $post().title)), // type error: a case child takes no value
  default_(() => 'No post')
)

show_match_(
  when_($post, () => b()(() => $post()?.title)),
  default_(() => 'No post')
)
```

## `swap_`

`swap_` is the block `if_`, `switch_` and `match_` are built on: it renders a child decided by a value. Unlike a binding, which updates content in place, the child is built anew every time the value changes.

```ts
import { signal } from 'nanoviews/store'
import { swap_, b, i } from 'nanoviews'

const $tab = signal('list')

swap_($tab, tab => (
  tab === 'list'
    ? b()(tab)
    : i()(tab)
))
// <b>list</b>

$tab('grid')
// <i>grid</i>
```

## `for_`

`for_` renders a row for every item of an array and keeps the rows in step with it.

```ts
import { signal } from 'nanoviews/store'
import { for_, trackById, ul, li } from 'nanoviews'

const $players = signal([
  { id: 1, name: 'chopper' },
  { id: 2, name: 'magixx' },
  { id: 3, name: 'zont1x' }
])

ul()(
  for_($players, trackById)(
    $player => li()(() => $player().name)
  )
)
// <ul><li>chopper</li><li>magixx</li><li>zont1x</li></ul>
```

### Trackers

The second argument is a tracker: it names a row, so on reorder the row's DOM, signals and effects move with it instead of being rebuilt. Reversing the list above:

```ts
$players(players => [...players].reverse())
// <ul><li>zont1x</li><li>magixx</li><li>chopper</li></ul>
```

The three `li` elements are the ones built at first: the rows moved, and nothing was rebuilt.

`trackById` names a row by the `id` of its item, and `trackBy(key)` makes a tracker for another key: `for_($cities, trackBy('label'))`. Any function of the item and its index works too: `for_($files, file => file.path)`.

Without a tracker a row is named by its position. A reorder leaves every row where it is and writes the item of the new position into it, so whatever a row holds of its own, a local signal or the state of an input, stays with the position, not with the item. Give a tracker whenever the items are objects or the rows hold state.

### Row Arguments

The render is given the row, its index signal and the key the tracker named the row by. The index changes while the row moves, the key never does. Without a tracker the key is the index.

```ts
ul()(
  for_($players, trackById)(
    ($player, $index, id) => li()(
      $index, ': ', () => $player().name, ' #', id
    )
  )
)
// <ul><li>0: chopper #1</li><li>1: magixx #2</li><li>2: zont1x #3</li></ul>

$players(players => [...players].reverse())
// <ul><li>0: zont1x #3</li><li>1: magixx #2</li><li>2: chopper #1</li></ul>
```

### Writable Rows

When the list is a writable signal, so is the row: writing the row writes a new item into a new array, and everything that reads the list follows. `record` turns the row into writable fields, ready for two-way bindings.

```ts
import { signal, record } from 'nanoviews/store'
import { for_, trackById, ul, li, label, input } from 'nanoviews'

interface Todo {
  id: number
  title: string
  done: boolean
}

const $todos = signal<Todo[]>([
  { id: 1, title: 'Write docs', done: false },
  { id: 2, title: 'Ship it', done: false }
])

ul()(
  for_($todos, trackById)(
    ($todo) => {
      const { $title, $done } = record($todo)

      return (
        li()(
          label()(
            input({
              type: 'checkbox',
              checked: $done
            }),
            $title
          )
        )
      )
    }
  )
)
// <ul><li><label><input type="checkbox">Write docs</label></li><li><label><input type="checkbox">Ship it</label></li></ul>
```

Ticking the first box writes `{ id: 1, title: 'Write docs', done: true }` into a new `$todos` array.

A list that cannot be written, such as a `computed` list, hands out read-only rows: there is nothing to write back to. In the types, the rows of a signal typed `T[] | null` or `T[] | undefined`, such as `signal<Todo[]>()`, are read-only too. Keep a list you edit through its rows non-nullable, with `[]` for no items, or type it with `EmptyValue` from `nanoviews/store`: the rows of `signal<Todo[] | EmptyValue>(null)` are writable.

### Read the Row, Not the List

Inside a row, read the row's own signals, `$item()` and `$index()`. A read of the whole list there, `$items()`, subscribes every row to every change of the list, so one edited item re-runs that read in every row. A value derived from the whole list belongs outside the rows, in a computed the rows read: `length` notifies only when the length changes.

```ts
import { length } from 'nanoviews/store'
import { for_, trackById, ul, li } from 'nanoviews'

const $total = length($players)

ul()(
  for_($players, trackById)(
    ($player, $index) => li()(
      () => $index() + 1, ' of ', $total, ': ', () => $player().name
    )
  )
)
// <ul><li>1 of 3: chopper</li><li>2 of 3: magixx</li><li>3 of 3: zont1x</li></ul>
```

### Selection

One `selector` outside the loop, asked by key in each row, marks the selected row: a change of the selection wakes the row that lost it and the row that got it, and no other, where a computed per row would wake them all.

### Empty State

The second function of the row call renders the empty state: for an empty array, and for `null` or `undefined`. It stays while the list stays empty and gives way to the rows when items arrive.

```ts
import { signal } from 'nanoviews/store'
import { for_, ul, li } from 'nanoviews'

const $results = signal<string[] | null>(null)

ul()(
  for_($results)(
    $result => li()($result),
    () => li()('Nothing found')
  )
)
// <ul><li>Nothing found</li></ul>

$results(['Berlin', 'Prague'])
// <ul><li>Berlin</li><li>Prague</li></ul>

$results([])
// <ul><li>Nothing found</li></ul>
```

### Static Arrays

A plain array takes no tracker and renders once. The row gets the plain item, its index and the index again as its key.

```ts
import { for_, ul, li } from 'nanoviews'

const links = ['Home', 'Blog', 'About']

ul()(
  for_(links)(
    link => li()(link),
    () => li()('No links')
  )
)
// <ul><li>Home</li><li>Blog</li><li>About</li></ul>
```

### Duplicate Keys

Keys must be unique within the list. A repeated key is not reported: the loop holds one row per key, so depending on where the repeat falls, the list renders a row short, or the write throws a `TypeError` from inside the loop and leaves the old rows on screen. When values can repeat, track by something that cannot, or give no tracker and let the positions name the rows:

```ts
import { signal } from 'nanoviews/store'
import { for_, ul, li } from 'nanoviews'

const $tags = signal(['news', 'tech', 'news'])

ul()(
  for_($tags)(
    $tag => li()($tag)
  )
)
// <ul><li>news</li><li>tech</li><li>news</li></ul>
```

With `tag => tag` as the tracker, the same list renders `<ul><li>news</li><li>tech</li></ul>`.

### `as_`

`as_` hands the row through a transform before rendering it, carrying the index and the key through. Here the rows of the same `$players` list become records:

```ts
import { record } from 'nanoviews/store'
import { for_, trackById, as_, ul, li } from 'nanoviews'

ul()(
  for_($players, trackById)(
    as_(record, ($player, $index) => li()(
      $index, ': ', $player.$name
    ))
  )
)
// <ul><li>0: chopper</li><li>1: magixx</li><li>2: zont1x</li></ul>
```

The transformed row is still bound to the list: a write to `$player.$name` lands in `$players`.

## `throw_`

`throw_` throws an error from inside an expression, where a `throw` statement cannot stand.

```ts
import { ul, component$, throw_ } from 'nanoviews'

const List = component$((_, children) => (
  ul()(
    ...children.length ? children : throw_(new Error('Children are required'))
  )
))
```

`List()` without children throws `Children are required` when it is built.

---

# Forms

Bind the value, the check and the selection of form controls to signals.

`input`, `textarea` and `select` bind their state through the DOM properties, not the attributes, so what the user does and what the signal holds stay one thing. Every binding on this page takes its value in one of three forms:

- A plain value is set once, when the control is built.
- An accessor is followed: every new value is written to the control.
- A writable signal is followed as well, and it also receives what the user types or picks.

| Binding                                              | Controls                      | Writes back on       |
| ---------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------- | -------------------- |
| [`value`](#value)                                    | text inputs, `textarea`       | `input`              |
| [`checked`](#checked)                                | checkbox, radio button        | `change`             |
| [`value`](#select)                                   | `select`                      | `change`             |
| [`defaultValue`](#defaultvalue-and-defaultchecked)   | `input`, `textarea`, `select` | never, it is one way |
| [`defaultChecked`](#defaultvalue-and-defaultchecked) | checkbox, radio button        | never, it is one way |

Every other attribute of a control is an attribute, as on any element.

## `value`

`value` of a text input or a `textarea` is the text in the control. A writable signal is two-way: writing it updates the control, and every `input` event writes the text back into it.

```ts
import { signal } from 'nanoviews/store'
import { input, textarea } from 'nanoviews'

const $name = signal('')
const $review = signal('')

input({
  type: 'text',
  value: $name
})

textarea({
  name: 'review',
  value: $review
})
```

A plain value is written to the property once, when the control is built, and never becomes the `value` attribute. What the user types stays in the control:

```ts
import { input } from 'nanoviews'

input({
  type: 'text',
  value: 'Hello'
})
// <input type="text">
```

A read-only accessor, a computed say, only drives the control: what the user types stays in it until the accessor changes, and nothing is written back.

```ts
import { signal, computed } from 'nanoviews/store'
import { input } from 'nanoviews'

const $firstName = signal('Ada')
const $lastName = signal('Lovelace')
const $fullName = computed(() => `${$firstName()} ${$lastName()}`)

input({
  type: 'text',
  value: $fullName
})
```

`null` and `undefined` are an empty text. A plain `value` may also be a number, but a signal or an accessor holds a string, since a string is what the user types: a signal of a number is a type error. For a number, keep the text in the signal and derive the number from it:

```ts
import { signal, computed } from 'nanoviews/store'
import { input } from 'nanoviews'

const $ageText = signal('18')
const $age = computed(() => parseFloat($ageText()))

input({
  type: 'number',
  value: $ageText
})
```

While the field holds no number yet, empty or a lone `-` the user is typing, its `value` is `''` and `$age` is `NaN`. A number signal fed from `onInput` with `valueAsNumber` instead would turn that moment into `NaN`, and the binding would erase the `-`.

## Key Order

Attributes are applied in the order of the keys, and for a control the order can matter.

A `range` input clamps its value to the `min` and `max` it has at the moment the value is written, so the bounds go before `value` and `defaultValue`:

```ts
import { signal } from 'nanoviews/store'
import { input } from 'nanoviews'

const $volume = signal('150')

input({
  type: 'range',
  min: 0,
  max: 200,
  step: 10,
  value: $volume
})
```

With `value` first, the control would still have the default bounds, 0 and 100, when the value lands, and would show 100 while the signal holds `'150'`.

A handler for the event a binding listens to, `onInput` for `value` and `onChange` for `checked` or a `select`, sees the new value in the signal only when it stands after the binding. In front of the binding the handler runs first, while the signal still holds the previous value. `event.target` has the new value either way.

```ts
import { signal } from 'nanoviews/store'
import { input } from 'nanoviews'

const $query = signal('')

input({
  type: 'search',
  value: $query,
  onInput() {
    search($query()) // the text the user has just typed
  }
})
```

## `textarea`

`textarea` takes no children: its text is its `value`, or its `defaultValue`. Like `input`, it is described in a single call, and a children call is a type error.

```ts
import { textarea } from 'nanoviews'

textarea({
  name: 'review',
  rows: 4,
  defaultValue: 'Write your review here'
})
// <textarea name="review" rows="4">Write your review here</textarea>
```

## `checked`

`checked` binds a checkbox or a radio button the same way, through the `checked` property. A writable signal receives the check on every `change` event:

```ts
import { signal } from 'nanoviews/store'
import { input } from 'nanoviews'

const $agree = signal(false)

input({
  type: 'checkbox',
  checked: $agree
})
```

### `Indeterminate`

The `Indeterminate` symbol is the [third state](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/input/checkbox#indeterminate_state_checkboxes) of a checkbox. It sets the `indeterminate` property and leaves the check underneath as it was, and a boolean clears it. A click of the user clears it too, and a writable signal receives the boolean the click left. A signal that holds the third state is typed with the symbol:

```ts
import { signal } from 'nanoviews/store'
import { input, Indeterminate } from 'nanoviews'

const $checked = signal<boolean | typeof Indeterminate>(false)

input({
  type: 'checkbox',
  checked: $checked
})

$checked(Indeterminate)
```

### Radio Buttons

The radio button the user leaves by picking another one in its group gets no `change` event, so a writable signal per button would keep `true` for the button that lost the check. Bind the group to one signal instead: `checked` of every button follows a comparison with `is`, and `onChange` writes the pick.

```ts
import { signal, is } from 'nanoviews/store'
import { label, input, fragment } from 'nanoviews'

const $plan = signal('free')

fragment(
  label()(
    input({
      type: 'radio',
      name: 'plan',
      value: 'free',
      checked: is($plan, 'free'),
      onChange() {
        $plan('free')
      }
    }),
    ' Free'
  ),
  label()(
    input({
      type: 'radio',
      name: 'plan',
      value: 'pro',
      checked: is($plan, 'pro'),
      onChange() {
        $plan('pro')
      }
    }),
    ' Pro'
  )
)
```

## `select`

`value` on a `select` is the value of the selected option. A writable signal receives the pick on every `change` event:

```ts
import { signal } from 'nanoviews/store'
import { select, option } from 'nanoviews'

const $position = signal('mid')

select({
  name: 'position',
  value: $position
})(
  option({
    value: 'carry'
  })(
    'Yatoro'
  ),
  option({
    value: 'mid'
  })(
    'Larl'
  ),
  option({
    value: 'offlane'
  })(
    'Collapse'
  )
)
```

### `multiple`

Under `multiple: true`, `value` is the list of the selected values, and a writable signal receives the list:

```ts
import { signal } from 'nanoviews/store'
import { select, option } from 'nanoviews'

const $positions = signal(['mid', 'carry'])

select({
  name: 'positions',
  multiple: true,
  value: $positions
})(
  option({
    value: 'carry'
  })(
    'Yatoro'
  ),
  option({
    value: 'mid'
  })(
    'Larl'
  ),
  option({
    value: 'offlane'
  })(
    'Collapse'
  )
)
```

`multiple` decides the shape of `value`, so it is written as a plain `true`: a list on a single select, or a single value under `multiple: true`, is a type error. A `multiple` that follows an accessor takes either shape, and a writable signal receives the shape the select has at the moment of the change.

## `defaultValue` and `defaultChecked`

The default of a control, what a form reset returns it to, is set apart from its value, the React way: `defaultValue` on `input`, `textarea` and `select`, `defaultChecked` on a checkbox or a radio button. They are one way: a plain value is set once, an accessor is followed, and what the user does never goes back into it.

```ts
import { form, input, textarea, select, option, button } from 'nanoviews'

form()(
  input({
    type: 'text',
    defaultValue: 'Yatoro'
  }),
  input({
    type: 'checkbox',
    defaultChecked: true
  }),
  textarea({
    defaultValue: 'Write your review here'
  }),
  select({
    defaultValue: 'mid'
  })(
    option({
      value: 'carry'
    })(
      'Yatoro'
    ),
    option({
      value: 'mid'
    })(
      'Larl'
    )
  ),
  button({
    type: 'reset'
  })(
    'Reset'
  )
)
```

On a `select`, `defaultValue` marks its options the way `value` selects them, a plain one a microtask after the build. A bound `value` leaves the default alone. A reset fires no `input` or `change` event, so a writable signal bound to `value` or `checked` keeps what it held while the control goes back to its default.

## Files

Files have no binding: read `event.target.files` in the `onChange` handler of a file input.

```ts
import { input } from 'nanoviews'

input({
  type: 'file',
  accept: 'image/*',
  multiple: true,
  onChange(event) {
    upload(event.target.files)
  }
})
```

`event.target` is typed by the element, so `files` is a `FileList | null` here.
