# Dependency Injection

Share stores and services across a view tree with context$, provide and inject, and swap them for a subtree, a test or a story.

Dependency injection lets a view tree share stores and services without keeping them in module scope. A component asks for a dependency by its factory, and the context it is built in decides which instance it gets. A subtree, a test or a story can swap a dependency for another value, and every app instance gets stores of its own.

Nanoviews uses the dependency injection of its reactive core, the one Nano Kit is built on. `inject`, `provide`, `provideAs`, `InjectionContext`, `Injectable$` and `DependencyNotFound` come from `nanoviews/store`; `context$` and `isolate$`, which choose the context a part of the view is built in, come from `nanoviews`.

```ts
import { signal, provide, inject } from 'nanoviews/store'
import { div, component$, context$, mount } from 'nanoviews'

type Theme = 'light' | 'dark'

function Theme$() {
  return signal<Theme>('light')
}

const Themed = component$(() => {
  const $theme = inject(Theme$)

  return (
    div()(
      'Current theme: ', $theme
    )
  )
})

const App = component$(() => {
  const $theme = signal<Theme>('dark')

  return (
    context$(provide(Theme$, $theme))(
      Themed()
    )
  )
})

mount(App, document.querySelector('#app')!)
// <div>Current theme: dark</div>
```

`Themed` asks for `Theme$` and gets the signal that `App` provides. Nano Kit's documentation covers the same system from the store side: [Dependency Injection](https://nano-kit.js.org/store/core-concepts/#dependency-injection).

## DI Basics

Factories, providers and tokens work in a view the way they do anywhere else, and Nano Kit's docs cover them:

| API                           | What it does                                                                                                                        | Nano Kit docs                                                                                   |
| ----------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `inject(Factory$)`            | the instance of the current context, made by the factory, a `Name$` function, on first use; what the factory returns is the default | [Dependency Injection](https://nano-kit.js.org/store/core-concepts/#dependency-injection)       |
| nested contexts               | an instance lives in the deepest context that provides something it read, and the contexts below share it                           | [Nested Contexts](https://nano-kit.js.org/store/core-concepts/#nested-contexts)                 |
| `provide(Factory$, value)`    | a provider for `context$`: `inject` returns the value there; it fits the factory's type exactly, a signal included                  | [Providing Custom Values](https://nano-kit.js.org/store/core-concepts/#providing-custom-values) |
| `provideAs(Factory$, Other$)` | resolves a factory as another one, which shares its instance: a mock API in stories and tests                                       | [Aliases](https://nano-kit.js.org/store/core-concepts/#aliases)                                 |
| `Injectable$`                 | a class as the token, made with `new`                                                                                               | [Class Tokens](https://nano-kit.js.org/store/core-concepts/#class-tokens)                       |
| `DependencyNotFound`          | thrown by a factory with no default, so a missing provider fails at the first `inject`                                              | [Required Dependencies](https://nano-kit.js.org/store/core-concepts/#required-dependencies)     |

## `context$`

`context$(...providers)(child)` describes a child built within an injection context. The child is built inside the context, wherever its description was made, and every `inject` in it, however deep, sees the values of that context. Which context it is depends on what `context$` is given and on what is above it.

### Root Context

An app opens one context at its root before anything injects. `context$()` with no context above opens the root context, and the app wraps its whole view in it, here with `Themed` from above:

```ts
import { main, component$, context$, mount } from 'nanoviews'

const App = component$(() => (
  context$()(
    main()(
      Themed()
    )
  )
))

mount(App, document.querySelector('#app')!)
// <main><div>Current theme: light</div></main>
```

A `context$` with providers and no context above opens the root context too, with those providers in it. With no context at all, `inject` throws, so a missing root context shows up at the first component that injects. In development the error reads `Cannot inject dependency outside of injection context`; the production build skips that check, and the call fails with a `TypeError` there.

### Child Context

`context$` with providers inside a context opens a child context: its providers override the values above, and everything else is inherited. A component provides to its own children the same way, wrapping them in `context$`:

```ts
import { type WritableSignal, signal, provide, inject, is } from 'nanoviews/store'
import { type ComponentInstance, div, button, component$, context$ } from 'nanoviews'

function Selected$() {
  return signal('')
}

const SegmentedControl = component$((
  { $value }: { $value: WritableSignal<string> },
  children: ComponentInstance[]
) => (
  context$(provide(Selected$, $value))(
    div({
      role: 'tablist'
    })(
      ...children
    )
  )
))

const Segment = component$(({ value }: { value: string }, children) => {
  const $selected = inject(Selected$)

  return (
    button({
      role: 'tab',
      'aria-selected': is($selected, value),
      onClick() {
        $selected(value)
      }
    })(
      ...children
    )
  )
})

const $tab = signal('signals')

SegmentedControl({
  $value: $tab
})(
  Segment({
    value: 'signals'
  })(
    'Signals'
  ),
  Segment({
    value: 'log'
  })(
    'Log'
  )
)
// <div role="tablist"><button role="tab" aria-selected="true">Signals</button><button role="tab" aria-selected="false">Log</button></div>
```

The `Segment()` instances are created as arguments of the `SegmentedControl` call, outside its context, and still inject what it provides: an instance renders when it is built, and it is built inside `context$`. A click on `Log` writes `$tab`, and the selection follows.

`context$` takes one child. Several children go under an element, as here, or under a `fragment`.

### Current Context

Inside a context, `context$()` with no providers adds nothing: the child is built in the current context. So a component that opens the root context for itself can also be built inside a context made around it, by a test or a host page, and then uses that one:

```ts
const App = component$(() => (
  context$()(
    Themed()
  )
))

mount(() => context$(provide(Theme$, signal<Theme>('dark')))(
  App()
), document.querySelector('#app')!)
// <div>Current theme: dark</div>
```

Writing Tests shows how tests use this to override dependencies.

## `InjectionContext`

`context$` also takes an `InjectionContext` instance in place of the providers. The child is built within that very context: it sees the values of the instance and of the parent it was created with, not those of the context around the call. This is how a context made outside the view is handed to it, so the view and the code around it share the same instances:

```ts
import { InjectionContext, signal, provide, inject } from 'nanoviews/store'
import { context$, mount } from 'nanoviews'

const context = new InjectionContext([
  provide(Theme$, signal<Theme>('dark'))
])

mount(() => context$(context)(
  Themed()
), document.querySelector('#app')!)
// <div>Current theme: dark</div>

const $theme = inject(Theme$, context)

$theme('light')
// <div>Current theme: light</div>
```

`new InjectionContext(providers, parent)` takes the providers, if any, and an optional parent context. `inject(Factory$, context)` resolves in the given context outside any render: it returns the instance the view injects, and creates it there when the view has not asked for it yet. Tests use the same pair to reach the stores of the view they render.

## `isolate$`

`isolate$(child)` builds a child outside any injection context, so nothing above it is reachable. It does not fall back to the defaults: `inject` right inside a bare `isolate$` throws. A `context$` inside it starts a fresh tree that inherits nothing:

```ts
import { signal, provide, inject } from 'nanoviews/store'
import { div, component$, context$, isolate$ } from 'nanoviews'

type Theme = 'light' | 'dark'

function Theme$() {
  return signal<Theme>('light')
}

const Themed = component$(() => {
  const $theme = inject(Theme$)

  return (
    div()(
      'Theme: ', $theme
    )
  )
})

const App = component$(() => (
  context$(provide(Theme$, signal<Theme>('dark')))(
    div()(
      Themed(),
      isolate$(
        context$()(
          Themed()
        )
      )
    )
  )
))
// <div><div>Theme: dark</div><div>Theme: light</div></div>
```

The isolated `context$()` opens a new root, where `Theme$` has its default again. Use `isolate$` where a subtree must start from scratch, with new instances of every dependency.

## Inject During Render

`inject` works only synchronously while a view is built: in a render, in a branch or a row a block builds, and in a factory that another `inject` runs. Inside an `effect$`, an event handler, a promise callback or a timer there is no current context, and it throws. Inject everything a component needs in its body and close over the results:

```ts
const ThemeToggle = component$(() => {
  const $theme = inject(Theme$)

  return (
    button({
      onClick() {
        $theme(theme => theme === 'light' ? 'dark' : 'light')
      }
    })(
      'Theme: ', $theme
    )
  )
})
```

---

# SVG

Draw SVG with the factories of the nanoviews/svg entry point.

SVG elements live in the `nanoviews/svg` entry point, so their code stays out of the bundle of an app that never draws one. `nanoviews` itself has no SVG factories.

## Elements

Every SVG tag has a factory in `nanoviews/svg`, with the same call shape as the HTML ones: the attributes in the first call, the children in the second. The elements are created in the SVG namespace, and signals and accessors bind the way they do in HTML:

```ts
import { signal } from 'nanoviews/store'
import { svg, circle, path } from 'nanoviews/svg'

const $radius = signal(10)

svg({
  viewBox: '0 0 24 24',
  width: 24,
  height: 24
})(
  circle({
    cx: 12,
    cy: 12,
    r: $radius,
    fill: 'none',
    stroke: 'currentColor',
    strokeWidth: 2
  }),
  path({
    d: 'M8 12l3 3 5-6',
    fill: 'none',
    stroke: 'currentColor'
  })
)
// <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" width="24" height="24"><circle cx="12" cy="12" r="10" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"></circle><path d="M8 12l3 3 5-6" fill="none" stroke="currentColor"></path></svg>
```

Shapes and leaves are void: one call, no children. These are `circle`, `ellipse`, `line`, `path`, `polygon`, `polyline`, `rect`, `image`, `use`, `mpath` and the animation elements `animate`, `animateMotion`, `animateTransform` and `set`. Children passed to them are a type error.

## Attributes

Attribute names are camelCase, as in React. Presentation attributes, the ones that double as CSS properties, reach the DOM hyphenated: `strokeWidth` as `stroke-width`, `fillOpacity` as `fill-opacity`, `textAnchor` as `text-anchor`, `clipPath` as `clip-path`. The rest keep their SVG spelling: `viewBox`, `preserveAspectRatio`, `gradientUnits`, and the camelCase names that share a prefix with presentation ones, such as `markerWidth`, `textLength` and `clipPathUnits`. `tabIndex` and `crossOrigin` are written in lowercase, as in HTML.

The camelCase name is the only spelling: a dashed key such as `'stroke-width'` is a type error. References use `href`, which replaces `xlinkHref`:

```ts
import { svg, defs, symbol, path, use } from 'nanoviews/svg'

svg({
  viewBox: '0 0 48 24',
  width: 48,
  height: 24
})(
  defs()(
    symbol({
      id: 'check',
      viewBox: '0 0 24 24'
    })(
      path({
        d: 'M5 12l5 5 9-10',
        fill: 'none',
        stroke: 'currentColor',
        strokeWidth: 2,
        strokeLinecap: 'round'
      })
    )
  ),
  use({
    href: '#check',
    width: 24,
    height: 24
  }),
  use({
    href: '#check',
    x: 24,
    width: 24,
    height: 24
  })
)
// <svg viewBox="0 0 48 24" width="48" height="24"><defs><symbol id="check" viewBox="0 0 24 24"><path d="M5 12l5 5 9-10" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round"></path></symbol></defs><use href="#check" width="24" height="24"></use><use href="#check" x="24" width="24" height="24"></use></svg>
```

The SVG 1.1 font, glyph and color profile attributes are not typed. ARIA attributes keep their dashed names, `'aria-label'` say, as on HTML elements, while `data-*` is typed on HTML elements only.

## HTML in `foreignObject`

HTML inside `foreignObject` comes from `nanoviews`: an HTML factory creates an HTML element wherever it is inserted.

```ts
import { div } from 'nanoviews'
import { svg, foreignObject } from 'nanoviews/svg'

svg({
  viewBox: '0 0 200 100'
})(
  foreignObject({
    x: 0,
    y: 0,
    width: 200,
    height: 100
  })(
    div({
      class: 'note'
    })(
      'HTML inside'
    )
  )
)
// <svg viewBox="0 0 200 100"><foreignObject x="0" y="0" width="200" height="100"><div class="note">HTML inside</div></foreignObject></svg>
```

## Bindings and Events

`ref`, `style` objects, `autoFocus` and `class` lists work on SVG elements the way they do on HTML ones, and so do event handlers (see Core Concepts):

```ts
import { signal, when } from 'nanoviews/store'
import { svg, path } from 'nanoviews/svg'

const $active = signal(false)
const $icon = signal<SVGSVGElement | null>(null)

svg({
  ref: $icon,
  viewBox: '0 0 24 24',
  class: ['icon', when($active, 'icon_active')],
  style: {
    color: 'tomato'
  },
  onClick() {
    $active(active => !active)
  }
})(
  path({
    d: 'M4 12h16',
    stroke: 'currentColor'
  })
)
// <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" class="icon" style="color: tomato;"><path d="M4 12h16" stroke="currentColor"></path></svg>
```

A `ref` is checked against the element here too: `$icon` fits `svg`, and a signal of another element is a type error.

## Types

`nanoviews/svg` exports its types under the same names as the HTML ones in `nanoviews`: `Attributes<'circle'>` for the attributes of an element, `ElementName` for the tag names, `PickElementType<'circle'>` for the element, `IntrinsicElements` for the map of tags to elements, `ElementFactory` and `VoidElementFactory` for the factories. A component that passes attributes on to an SVG element types them the same way:

```ts
import { component$ } from 'nanoviews'
import { type Attributes, svg, path } from 'nanoviews/svg'

interface IconProps extends Attributes<'svg'> {
  d: string
}

const Icon = component$(({ d, ...props }: IconProps) => (
  svg({
    viewBox: '0 0 24 24',
    width: 24,
    height: 24,
    ...props
  })(
    path({
      d,
      fill: 'currentColor'
    })
  )
))

Icon({
  d: 'M4 4h16v16H4z',
  class: 'icon'
})
// <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" width="24" height="24" class="icon"><path d="M4 4h16v16H4z" fill="currentColor"></path></svg>
```

In a module that imports the HTML types too, alias one of them: `import type { Attributes as SvgAttributes } from 'nanoviews/svg'`.

# Advanced

Use raw HTML, shadow DOM and portals, write element behaviors of your own, and learn the order of effects, the batching rules, the TypeScript types and the limits of Nanoviews.

## `dangerouslySetInnerHtml`

`dangerouslySetInnerHtml` describes an element whose inner HTML is set from a string once the element is built. It takes the description of the element and the HTML, a static string or an accessor to follow:

```ts
import { signal } from 'nanoviews/store'
import { div, dangerouslySetInnerHtml } from 'nanoviews'

const $html = signal('<p>Some text</p>')

dangerouslySetInnerHtml(
  div({
    class: 'markdown'
  }),
  $html
)
// <div class="markdown"><p>Some text</p></div>
```

A new string in the signal replaces the content. The result describes the element and takes no children call: the HTML is its content. The element may come from any function that returns one, `() => document.createElement('x-markdown')` say, for a tag that has no factory.

> Caution: The HTML is inserted as it is. Markup from a source that is not trusted, such as user input, must be sanitized before it gets here.

## `shadow`

`shadow` describes a host element with a [shadow root](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Web_components/Using_shadow_DOM). It takes the host the way `dangerouslySetInnerHtml` takes its element, the options of [`attachShadow`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Element/attachShadow), and then the children like an element. On build it attaches the root and puts the children into it:

```ts
import { div, style, shadow } from 'nanoviews'

shadow(
  div({
    id: 'card'
  }),
  {
    mode: 'open'
  }
)(
  style()(':host { display: block; padding: 1rem }'),
  'Rendered in the shadow root'
)
// <div id="card"></div>
```

The host stays empty in the document, and the children, bindings and blocks included, live in its shadow root, where the `style` element applies to them alone. The host must be an element that allows a shadow root: a custom element, `article`, `aside`, `blockquote`, `body`, `div`, `footer`, `h1` to `h6`, `header`, `main`, `nav`, `p`, `section` or `span`. On any other element `attachShadow` throws a `NotSupportedError` when the host is built. A custom element comes from a function: `shadow(() => document.createElement('user-card'), { mode: 'open' })`.

## `portal`

`portal` renders a child in another place in the DOM. It describes an empty child: on build it calls the target function and mounts the child into the node it returns, so the target must exist by then. The child is removed with the part of the view that built the portal: the `if_` branch or `for_` row that holds it, or the whole view on unmount. A component that only portals returns `portal(...)`:

```ts
import { signal } from 'nanoviews/store'
import { div, portal, if_, component$ } from 'nanoviews'

const Toast = component$(() => (
  portal(
    () => document.body,
    div({
      class: 'toast'
    })(
      'Saved'
    )
  )
))

const $saved = signal(false)

div({
  class: 'editor'
})(
  if_($saved)(
    () => Toast()
  )
)
```

While `$saved` holds, the toast is the last child of `body`, and the editor has nothing in its place. Once `$saved` is false again, the toast is removed.

### Inside `show_`

`show_` parks its content instead of destroying it, and that does not suit a portal: hiding runs the removal, and showing again does not append the child back. Toggle a portalled tree the other way round, with `show_` inside the portal:

```ts
import { signal } from 'nanoviews/store'
import { portal, show_ } from 'nanoviews'

const $open = signal(false)

portal(
  () => document.body,
  show_($open, () => Modal())
)
```

While `$open` is false, the parked tree is out of the target, and it comes back with its state on show.

The same goes for `ref` under `show_`: the element is handed over once, when it is built, and hiding hands over `null`, so after the first hide the ref stays `null`. Use `if_` for a subtree whose `ref` matters: every build hands the new element over.

## Batching

A write to a signal flushes at once: the effects and bindings that depend on it run before the write returns. Some writes are held instead, so what depends on them runs once, after all of them:

- `mount` batches the writes made while the view is built, while its effects first run and while it unmounts.
- A write made by an effect that runs from a flush joins that flush: what it wakes runs after the effect returns, a single time for all its writes, and a `batch` there flushes nothing. Every re-run of an effect runs from a flush, and so does the first run of the effects a write brings in with a new branch or row.
- Everywhere else every write flushes on its own: in event handlers, timers and promise callbacks, and in the first run of a store `effect` created outside a flush or a batch, at module level say. Wrap several writes in `batch`.

```ts
import { signal, batch } from 'nanoviews/store'
import { button, component$, effect$ } from 'nanoviews'

const Rename = component$(() => {
  const $firstName = signal('John')
  const $lastName = signal('Doe')

  effect$(() => {
    console.log(`${$firstName()} ${$lastName()}`)
  })

  return (
    button({
      onClick() {
        batch(() => {
          $firstName('Jane')
          $lastName('Smith')
        })
      }
    })(
      'Rename'
    )
  )
})
```

A click logs `Jane Smith` once. Without `batch`, it would log `Jane Doe` first. Cases of a `match_` that move together are worth a `batch` for the same reason: without one, every write swaps the content.

## TypeScript Types

`nanoviews` exports the types of its API. These are the ones application code reaches for. `Signalish`, `Accessor`, `ReadableSignal` and `WritableSignal` come from `nanoviews/store` (see Reactivity), and `nanoviews/svg` exports `Attributes`, `ElementName`, `PickElementType`, `ElementFactory` and `VoidElementFactory` for SVG elements under the same names (see SVG).

```ts
import { type Attributes, type KeyboardEvent, input, component$ } from 'nanoviews'

interface SearchFieldProps extends Attributes<'input'> {
  onEnter(query: string): void
}

const SearchField = component$(({ onEnter, ...props }: SearchFieldProps) => {
  function onKeyDown(event: KeyboardEvent<HTMLInputElement>) {
    if (event.key === 'Enter') {
      onEnter(event.target.value)
    }
  }

  return (
    input({
      type: 'search',
      ...props,
      onKeyDown
    })
  )
})
```

### Elements and Attributes

| Type                         | Description                                                                                                       |
| ---------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Attributes<Tag>`            | The attributes the factory of a tag takes: `Attributes<'button'>`.                                                |
| `HTMLAttributes<T>`          | The attributes every HTML element takes; the attributes of each element extend it, like `InputHTMLAttributes<T>`. |
| `AriaAttributes`, `AriaRole` | The `aria-*` attributes and the values of `role`.                                                                 |
| `ElementName`                | The tag names that have a factory.                                                                                |
| `PickElementType<Tag>`       | The DOM element of a tag: `PickElementType<'input'>` is `HTMLInputElement`.                                       |
| `ElementFactory<Tag>`        | An element factory, such as `div`: the type of a prop that takes one.                                             |
| `VoidElementFactory<Tag>`    | A factory of a void element, such as `input`.                                                                     |
| `LazyElement<T, C>`          | A description of an element: called with children it keeps them, called with none it builds `T`.                  |
| `LazyVoidElement<T>`         | A description of a void element: the call builds `T`.                                                             |
| `ClassValue`                 | A value of `class`: a string, an accessor of one, or a list of parts.                                             |
| `ClassPart`                  | A part of a `class` list: a string, a nested list, or an accessor of either.                                      |
| `ClassList<V>`               | What `classList` returns for the parts `V`: an accessor, a string, or either.                                     |
| `StyleValue`                 | A value of `style`: an object of properties, or an accessor of one.                                               |
| `CSSProperties`              | The object of `style`: camelCased properties and `--custom` properties.                                           |
| `ElementRef<T>`              | A value of `ref`: a callback or a writable signal that receives `T` or `null`.                                    |
| `Booleanish`                 | `boolean \| 'true' \| 'false'`, for attributes like `draggable`.                                                  |

### Children and Components

| Type                   | Description                                                                                                             |
| ---------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Child`                | Anything a parent takes as a child: a description, a node, a primitive, or an accessor of a primitive.                  |
| `Children`             | A list of children: `Child[]`.                                                                                          |
| `LazyChild<T>`         | A description: a function its parent builds instead of reading it as an accessor.                                       |
| `Component<P, C>`      | What `component$` returns: it takes the props `P`, then the children `C`.                                               |
| `ComponentInstance<C>` | An instance of a component, what `Component(props)` returns: a call with children keeps them, a call with none renders. |
| `Render<P, C>`         | The render a component is made from: `(props, children) => Child`.                                                      |
| `SlotComponent<P, C>`  | What `slot$` returns.                                                                                                   |
| `SlotInstance<P, C>`   | An instance of a slot: a `slots$` render gets one, or `undefined`, for each declared slot.                              |
| `SlotsRender<P, D>`    | The render `slots$` takes: the props, the declared slots in order, then the rest of the children.                       |

### Control Flow

| Type                                      | Description                                                                                                       |
| ----------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `SwitchCase<T>`                           | A case of `switch_` and `show_switch_`, made by `case_` or `default_`.                                            |
| `MatchCase<T, R>`                         | A case of `match_`, made by `when_`.                                                                              |
| `AnyMatchCase`                            | A case of `match_` for any value, the type of its parameters: a list of cases built ahead is an `AnyMatchCase[]`. |
| `ShowMatchCase`                           | A case of `show_match_`: its child takes no value.                                                                |
| `TruthySignalish<T>`, `FalsySignalish<T>` | The value `if_` hands to its branches, narrowed to its truthy or its falsy side.                                  |
| `TruthyAccessor<T>`, `FalsyAccessor<T>`   | The same narrowing for a value that has to be an accessor: anything else gives `never`.                           |

### Events

| Type                                                                                                                     | Description                                                                                                    |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Event<T>`, `MouseEvent<T>`, `KeyboardEvent<T>`, `PointerEvent<T>`, `FocusEvent<T>`, `ChangeEvent<T>`, `FormEvent<T>`... | The native event with `target` typed as `T`. Importing one hides the DOM type of the same name in that module. |
| `EventHandler<E>`, `MouseEventHandler<T>`, `KeyboardEventHandler<T>`...                                                  | The type of an `on*` handler.                                                                                  |
| `DOMAttributes<T>`                                                                                                       | The `on*` handlers every element takes.                                                                        |
| `ModifierKey`                                                                                                            | The key names `getModifierState` takes.                                                                        |

### Values

| Type                      | Description                                                                           |
| ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Primitive`               | `string \| number \| boolean \| EmptyValue`: what a text child and an attribute hold. |
| `EmptyValue`              | `undefined \| null \| void`.                                                          |
| `FalsyValue`              | `EmptyValue \| false \| '' \| 0`.                                                     |
| `NonEmptyValue<T>`        | `T` without its empty values.                                                         |
| `AccessibleProps<T>`      | `T` with every prop optional and `Signalish`.                                         |
| `Destroy`, `MaybeDestroy` | A cleanup function, and a cleanup function or nothing.                                |
| `EffectCallback`          | The body of an effect: `(warmup?: true) => MaybeDestroy`.                             |
| `AnyFn`, `AnyObject`      | Any function, any object.                                                             |
